video_title: Is there way more conventional geothermal than we thought?
gist: Zanskar CEO Carl Hyland and CTO Joel Edwards argue that the USGS's 2008 conventional-geothermal assessment — roughly 9,000 MW discovered plus 30,000 MW undiscovered — is built on 1970s-80s data and understates the US resource by roughly a factor of 30, with ~10x more undiscovered sites each holding ~10x more power, putting terawatts within reach using ordinary, financeable conventional drilling. They back it with three field results (a repowered New Mexico plant whose new well delivers over 100 MW thermal at the wellhead, a Nevada site, and a genuinely blind greenfield discovery near Tonopah), argue natural permeability will stay permanently cheaper than EGS-created permeability the way Ghawar still beats shale, and describe a rotating development-capital facility plus a 100 MW portfolio PPA with NV Energy driven by hyperscaler data-center demand.

insights.claim: The USGS's 2008 assessment — the last comprehensive one — put US conventional geothermal at about 9,000 MW discovered plus roughly 30,000 MW undiscovered, a theoretical ceiling of only 7-8% of current US electricity demand, which is why capital shifted to enhanced geothermal instead.
insights.speaker: David Roberts, host
insights.so_what: The official resource number is the reason conventional geothermal has been uninvestable at scale; if it is wrong, the entire sector's addressable market re-rates.
insights.quote: The last comprehensive assessment by the US Geological Survey in 2008 identified about 9,000 megawatts of discovered potential

insights.claim: Zanskar's central claim is that there are roughly 10 times more undiscovered geothermal sites than the USGS estimates AND that each produces roughly 10 times more energy — compounding to terawatts of potential, enough for all US electricity demand, reachable with conventional drilling techniques.
insights.speaker: David Roberts, host, summarizing Zanskar
insights.so_what: A ~30x upward revision of a firm, carbon-free baseload resource that requires no new drilling technology — the single highest-leverage claim in the episode if it survives third-party validation.

insights.claim: The 2008 USGS estimate rests on exploration data from the 1970s and 1980s, so the assessment is roughly 20 years old and the underlying data is 40-50 years old.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Establishes that the consensus resource number predates modern drilling, satellite data and machine learning — the core of the mispricing argument.
insights.quote: the estimate is 20 years old but the data the estimates are using I think dates back to like the 70s and 80s

insights.claim: The US has only about 36 operating geothermal fields totaling roughly 4 GW, up only about 1 GW in the past decade — a sector that has been structurally stalled, in Hyland's view, because the industry simply stopped looking after 1980s failures.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Frames stagnation as a search-effort problem rather than a geology problem, which is a solvable and fundable condition.
insights.quote: maybe the simplest answer I'd have to that is that we stopped looking

insights.claim: Roughly half of the ~36 US geothermal fields were found by accident — a farmer drilling for water or a gold company drilling for gold — and the other half had visible surface manifestations like boiling mud pots and fumaroles, meaning essentially zero of the global fleet was found by deliberate blind exploration.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The strongest single argument for massive undiscovered resource: the existing inventory is a sample of what happened to be obvious, not what exists.
insights.quote: half of them were almost found by accident

insights.claim: Hyland explicitly analogizes current geothermal resource skepticism to the late-1800s peak oil declarations for Pennsylvania, arguing the pattern of underestimating subsurface resources is recurrent across natural-resource industries.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A historical base rate that favors resource-expansion bets over depletion narratives in any under-explored subsurface industry.
insights.quote: It reminded us of messages that were communicated in the late 1800s about oil and gas

insights.claim: The 1970s-80s explorers drilled sequentially along mapped young fault zones in the western US and mostly missed, because geothermal systems crop up in non-obvious places — and that low hit rate created a false perception of scarcity that has propagated into every subsequent model.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific mechanism by which a sampling artifact became institutional consensus — the kind of error that creates durable mispricing.
insights.quote: That perception has fed all the subsequent modeling.

insights.claim: Zanskar's evidentiary base for the upward revision is having physically tested over 5 million acres in the last five years, producing a hit rate across a far larger sample than any prior assessment used.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The proprietary dataset is the asset — it is what makes the resource claim defensible and what a competitor cannot buy.
insights.quote: we've gone out and we've tested over 5 million acres over the last five years

insights.claim: The USGS is currently updating its Great Basin hydrothermal assessment, but Edwards expects it to remain constrained because it still relies on the same legacy benchmark dataset and cannot make predictions outside its prior space.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Investors waiting for an official resource re-rating should not expect it from the new USGS number — the validation will have to come from drilling results.
insights.quote: you're still working with the same legacy data set functionally that you worked with in 2008

insights.claim: Zanskar cannot share its data with the USGS because the agency's publication mandate would make its discovery sites public before leases are secured — a structural reason the official resource estimate will stay stale.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Creates a persistent information asymmetry between the private explorer and the public benchmark — good for Zanskar's land position, bad for sector-wide capital formation.
insights.quote: if we were to share, you know, then that would make all our sites public

insights.claim: Zanskar's founding insight was that modern neural networks — post-AlexNet 2012 and transformers 2017 — could finally handle the sparse, messy, unstructured data problem that defeated earlier statistical approaches to geothermal exploration.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Dates the technology unlock precisely — the same timing argument applies to other sparse-data subsurface industries (minerals, groundwater, carbon storage).
insights.quote: One of the founding insights for the company was seeing how quickly neural networks were evolving.

insights.claim: Hyland's mental model for the AI advantage is inference from partial observation: if a geothermal system is a cat underground and you can only see its ears at the surface, the model infers how big the animal is and where its tail lies from a fragment of the data.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A transferable framing for where AI creates real edge — completing a latent structure from sparse indirect signals, not just organizing old records.

insights.claim: Edwards is explicit that probabilistic models are not the moat — national labs, universities and other companies build them, and 'you could go into Claude right now and probably build a probabistic model of your own' — the defensible asset is the iterative loop between model predictions and field testing.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A blunt statement that in physical-resource AI the model commoditizes and the closed-loop field-verification dataset is what holds value — a test to apply to every 'AI for X' industrial startup.
insights.quote: you have to pair your model predictions with tests in the field of those predictions

insights.claim: Zanskar's models started out materially worse than expert human explorers when benchmarked against expert predictions, and only began outperforming in the last year or two.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: An unusually honest capability timeline — and a warning that industrial AI takes roughly five years of field data before it beats domain experts.
insights.quote: In the early days, our models were frankly much worse than expert explorers.

insights.claim: Edwards concedes Zanskar has missed far more often than it has hit, and that model performance improves non-monotonically — periods of successive hits alternate with cold slumps, producing a spiky, streaky discovery rate rather than a smooth curve.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Discovery lumpiness means single-quarter drilling results are noise — the right unit of evaluation is the portfolio and the multi-year hit rate.
insights.quote: And to be clear, we've missed way more than we've hit.

insights.claim: Model gains come from two independent sources — more data with the same architecture yields higher precision, and architecture changes with the same data also improve predictions — and apparent step-backs usually reflect a more honest estimate of uncertainty rather than a worse model.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Two compounding improvement vectors, and a reminder that calibration improvements can look like accuracy regressions to an outside observer.

insights.claim: Zanskar measures its hit rate two ways — whether a drilled well's temperature and permeability outcome falls within the model's predicted probability range and how close it lands to the median, and separately via a physical flow test that measures flow, heat content and volume per unit time.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A concrete diligence checklist for anyone underwriting AI-led exploration claims: calibration against stated probabilities, not just headline discoveries.

insights.claim: The same AI-for-exploration pitch is being run in mineral exploration by KoBold, where traditional discovery amounted to a person walking the surface looking for visible manifestations — an astonishingly analog process with a very low hit rate and correspondingly high per-discovery cost.
insights.speaker: David Roberts, host
insights.so_what: Identifies a repeatable template — AI applied to legacy analog exploration data — that is now being run across at least two separate resource sectors.

insights.claim: At Lightning Dock in New Mexico, Zanskar acquired a failing, underproducing geothermal field and within a year drilled a single deeper well that restored the plant to full nameplate capacity and made the facility profitable.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Proves a repeatable acquisition strategy — buy written-off geothermal assets where the model disagrees with the incumbent's resource assessment, then re-drill.

insights.claim: The Lightning Dock well proved potential as much as 10 to 40 times larger than initial industry estimates for that site, and Zanskar says the same under-assessment pattern applies across many other fields.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: If existing brownfield sites are undervalued by 10-40x, the cheapest exposure to the thesis is buying distressed operating geothermal assets, not greenfield exploration.
insights.quote: as much as 10 to 40 times more than the initial industry estimates were for that site

insights.claim: The new Lightning Dock well delivers over 100 MW of thermal energy at the wellhead — as much heat as a small modular nuclear reactor — from a single wellbore you can wrap your arms around, and it is the most productive pumped geothermal well in the US benchmarked against Nevada's 200+ published production wells.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland and Joel Edwards, Zanskar
insights.so_what: The SMR comparison is the relevant one for data-center buyers evaluating firm carbon-free heat and power per unit of capital — and it is available today rather than in the 2030s.
insights.quote: And that's as much heat as a small modular nuclear reactor would create.

insights.claim: The Lightning Dock well has run at full capacity for over 12 months with no temperature decline, and remains pump-limited — a stronger pump would allow materially higher flow rates than it currently produces.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland and Joel Edwards, Zanskar
insights.so_what: Twelve months of flat temperature is the key reservoir-durability datapoint offtakers need; pump-limitation implies further upside at trivial incremental capex.
insights.quote: It is actually still pump limited.

insights.claim: Big Blind in Nevada, west of Tonopah, is a genuine blind greenfield discovery — no prior wells, no surface manifestations — found from model predictions in late 2023, drilled in 2025, hitting commercial reservoir conditions at only 2,000 to 3,000 feet, with a heat-flow anomaly footprint larger than either Pumpernickel or Lightning Dock.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The proof point that matters: commercial conditions found with zero prior signal validates that the undiscovered-resource thesis is testable, not just modeled.

insights.claim: The first Pumpernickel well failed not on targeting but on drilling conditions — and Edwards notes the counterintuitive correlation that the better the geothermal resource, the harder it is to drill, because the open pathways that make it productive destabilize the well.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Means dry-hole statistics systematically understate discovery success — some 'failures' are actually resource hits that could not be completed.
insights.quote: It's actually sort of fairly correlated that the better the resource, the harder the drilling.

insights.claim: Zanskar made its first discoveries in late 2021 and has many undisclosed discoveries beyond the three public projects, with announcement timing gated by the land work required to assemble federal, state and private lease positions.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Public project count materially understates the pipeline; leasing cadence, not discovery cadence, is the observable that will reveal it.
insights.quote: So our first discoveries back towards the tail end of 2021.

insights.claim: Geothermal is importing the oil and gas drilling stack wholesale — PDC bits, directional drilling assemblies, mud motors and automated rigs — collapsing geothermal well times from 40, 50 or 60-plus days down to weeks.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland and Joel Edwards, Zanskar
insights.so_what: A direct read-through: the 15 years of shale-funded drilling R&D is now a free cost tailwind for geothermal, and oilfield service providers gain a new end market.
insights.quote: a well would take 40, 50, 60 plus days to drill in geothermal. And now those timelines are collapsing down to, you know, weeks

insights.claim: Zanskar has achieved 50% to sometimes 90% cost declines in exploration data collection by bringing drilling and data collection in-house and optimizing for which well types most efficiently vector toward a target.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Exploration cost, historically the killer of geothermal economics, is falling faster than drilling cost — the main lever on levelized cost of electricity.
insights.quote: we've seen significant cost declines, 50 to sometimes 90% cost declines

insights.claim: Depth cost is non-linear because two things scale together: rig time, described as operating a small city daily, and construction materials — cement and steel — since a well must be constructed, not merely bored.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Explains why shallow commercial conditions (2,000-3,000 ft at Big Blind) are disproportionately valuable relative to deep resources.

insights.claim: Hyland's stated target is to exit subsidy dependence entirely, claiming that with current off-the-shelf technology and Zanskar's own cost of capital, geothermal would already be cheaper than all other power sources unsubsidized if you knew exactly where to drill and never missed.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Reduces the entire cost problem to exploration accuracy — meaning model hit rate is the single variable determining whether geothermal becomes the cheapest firm power.
insights.quote: if you just knew exactly where to drill every time and you never missed, it would already be cheaper than all of those other power sources on an unsubsidized basis

insights.claim: Future cost declines come from five stacked sources: better and bigger resources, resources closer to existing grid infrastructure, faster cheaper drilling, AI applied to operations, and software deployed across development and asset operation.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Proximity to grid infrastructure as a screening criterion is the underappreciated one — interconnection cost is now a first-order site-selection variable.

insights.claim: Artificially created permeability in engineered geothermal systems is one to multiple orders of magnitude worse than natural permeability — fracking-style hairline cracks versus natural openings that can be cavern-sized.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A physical ceiling on EGS flow rates and therefore on EGS cost — the core bear case against the enhanced-geothermal investment thesis.
insights.quote: the type of permeability that we've been able to create artificially in engineered systems is an order of magnitude and sometimes multiple orders of magnitude less than the type of natural permeability that we find in the earth

insights.claim: Asked directly whether a good natural geothermal resource will always be cheaper than any conceivable EGS site, Hyland answers that it is definitely true today and probably indefinitely into the future.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A permanent, not transitional, cost hierarchy claim — if right, EGS is capped as a secondary technology rather than the sector's future.
insights.quote: Definitely true today and we think probably indefinitely into the future.

insights.claim: The supporting analogy is oil and gas: decades into the shale revolution, the conventional Ghawar field in Saudi Arabia still produces at a significantly lower cost per barrel than the best US unconventional shale fields — natural permeability beating induced permeability.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A well-tested precedent transferred to a new sector — the strongest single argument for prioritizing conventional geothermal exploration over engineered systems.
insights.quote: the conventional fields like the gaw oil field in Saudi Arabia still produce oil at a significantly lower cost per barrel than even our best unconventional shell fields

insights.claim: Against the skeptic case that only small leftover pockets remain, Hyland points out that one of the most valuable companies in history was created by an oil discovery made a hundred years after the first peak-oil declaration — Ghawar and Aramco — arguing the best resources are still ahead.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The explicit bull framing to institutional investors: this is a discovery business with Aramco-scale precedent, not a niche-site roll-up.
insights.quote: it's more likely that the best resources are still ahead of us

insights.claim: Edwards endorses Quaise's deep-drilling thesis on the grounds that conventional tools break down at extreme depth — scientific wells to 30,000-35,000 feet took years because bits died every few hundred feet and holes collapsed — while conventional oil and gas fields already operate to 20,000 feet.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Defines the depth boundary — roughly 20,000 ft — that separates today's financeable conventional geothermal from speculative deep-drilling technology bets.

insights.claim: Geothermal's historical financing problem was that traditional project finance required all exploration and wellfield risk to be retired before capital would arrive, forcing exploration to fund itself at punitive cost of capital and loading soft costs into the final levelized cost of electricity.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Names cost of capital, not geology, as a principal driver of geothermal's uncompetitive LCOE — meaning a financing innovation moves the cost curve as much as a technology one.

insights.claim: The key unlock with financiers was not accuracy but quantifiability — Hyland says lenders care more about whether you can robustly quantify the uncertainty than about what the actual hit rate is, because a quantified risk profile can be priced.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A generalizable insight for any frontier-asset class: statistical legibility, not performance, is what converts an uninvestable activity into a financeable one.
insights.quote: they care more about just can you actually quantify the uncertainty to a robust degree more so than what the actual accuracy is

insights.claim: Zanskar's development capital facility is a rotating fund that sits ahead of bank-style project finance: it proves out a resource, then is replaced on that project by cheaper debt and tax equity, recycling the capital back into earlier-stage projects, with an accordion feature allowing larger draws as facility asset value grows.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A replicable capital structure for pre-bankable resource development — the closest thing in the episode to a new financial product for the energy transition.

insights.claim: The facility manages exploration risk through portfolio diversification rather than per-project certainty — failures are absorbed by successes, with the statistical base rate determining how to size and diversify the portfolio.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Converts a binary wildcat risk into an insurable, poolable risk — the same transformation that made oil exploration and venture capital financeable.

insights.claim: Hyland's stated ambition is that quantifying industry-wide performance — including legacy-tool performance — turns geothermal into an investable asset class, and that the facility structure spreads beyond Zanskar.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Watch for third-party adoption of this structure as the leading indicator that geothermal capital formation has genuinely changed.
insights.quote: Our hope is that by quantifying not just our performance but really the industry even with legacy tools performance that you make this a more investable asset class.

insights.claim: Zanskar signed a 100 MW portfolio PPA with NV Energy, structured so the power can be delivered from any combination of a basket of already-discovered and leased sites rather than from a single well or from speculative future discoveries.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The portfolio PPA is the contractual counterpart to the portfolio financing — a template that lets pre-development resources sign firm offtake.
insights.quote: this is what they call a portfolio PPA

insights.claim: NV Energy's primary motivation for seeking geothermal is new hyperscaler data-center demand in its territory looking for carbon-free baseload — and another developer has signed roughly 150 MW with the same utility.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Direct confirmation that data-center load growth is now the marginal buyer setting geothermal procurement in Nevada — the clearest demand signal in the sector.
insights.quote: one of the primary reasons NV Energy was seeking out geothermal power is because of new hyperscaler demand in their geography

insights.claim: Selling to a regulated utility rather than a private offtaker lets geothermal monetize ancillary services on top of energy — spinning reserves and voltage support — because it is genuinely firm power.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Ancillary revenue stacking is a structural margin advantage geothermal holds over wind and solar PPAs — relevant to comparative project returns.

insights.claim: Demand is broadening past data centers to manufacturing facilities and to utilities seeking decarbonization or grid resilience — Zanskar's Lightning Dock output goes to PNM in New Mexico purely to meet that utility's own needs.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Suggests offtake demand is not a single-customer data-center bubble, reducing concentration risk in the revenue thesis.

insights.claim: No greenfield geothermal power plant has been commissioned in the United States in roughly ten years, and Zanskar's stated goal is to get half a dozen greenfield projects to commissioning within the next few years.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The single most trackable near-term milestone for the whole thesis — greenfield commissioning is what would prove the industry can actually scale.
insights.quote: it's been about 10 years since anybody has turned on a green field geothermal power plant in the United States

insights.claim: Geothermal has retained bipartisan support, tax credits and DOE engagement at a moment when wind and solar are being actively disadvantaged, because it is small-footprint, baseload, carbon-free, domestic and free of at-risk foreign supply chains.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A rare politically durable clean-energy exposure in the current US policy environment — the relative-policy-risk trade versus wind and solar.
insights.quote: geothermal has kind of remained a bipartisan love child

insights.claim: 90% of identified US geothermal resources sit on public land — mostly Bureau of Land Management acreage rather than national parks — making the federal government a single landlord that is simultaneously the sector's largest risk and its largest opportunity.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Single-counterparty land exposure means federal permitting policy is effectively a switch on the entire sector's growth rate — the key non-geological risk to underwrite.
insights.quote: 90% of identified geothermal resources are on public land

insights.claim: Both the Biden administration at the tail end of its term and the Trump administration in its early days improved geothermal permitting, giving the sector current tailwinds — but Edwards says the regulatory process remains slow and outdated from years of the industry being ignored.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Permitting streamlining, not resource or technology, is the identified trigger for a sector boom — a specific policy catalyst to watch.
insights.quote: if we can get that streamlined, the industry will boom.

insights.claim: Edwards flags an internal worry that geothermal may now be attracting too much attention, which could turn its current bipartisan immunity into the same political exposure wind and solar face.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: A candid acknowledgment that the policy premium embedded in geothermal valuations is a function of obscurity and may not survive scale.

insights.claim: Zanskar concedes the resource is a basin-and-range story confined to the US West for the next decade or potentially two, limited primarily by drilling costs rather than by geology.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: Sets a realistic geographic boundary on the thesis and makes drilling cost the gating variable for any expansion beyond the West.
insights.quote: For the next decade or potentially two, that's true. Primarily driven by drilling costs

insights.claim: Hyland's answer to geographic concentration is that if you hold a terawatt of the most cost-advantaged power on the planet, demand relocates to the supply rather than the reverse.
insights.speaker: Carl Hyland, CEO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The load-migration argument that underpins siting data centers and energy-intensive manufacturing in the intermountain West.
insights.quote: we also believe demand will come to where you are

insights.claim: Every deep scientific well drilled — the German well to 10-11 km and the deeper Russian well — unexpectedly hit water and wellbore stability problems, meaning permeability exists at depths where geologists assumed rock would be dry and sealed.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The strongest physical evidence that conventional geothermal could eventually work far outside the West — heat is a given, and permeability now appears less depth-limited than assumed.
insights.quote: all of those cases where they went deep, they all ran into conditions that they didn't expect

insights.claim: Because nobody has drilled below a certain depth in places like Iowa, subsurface conditions there are simply unknown, and Edwards argues it is likely rather than merely possible that permeability exists at some depth in geographies never considered geothermal.
insights.speaker: Joel Edwards, CTO Zanskar
insights.so_what: The long-dated optionality in the thesis — a genuinely national geothermal resource, contingent entirely on drilling cost declines.
